title: Aggregations and Grouping
subtitle: GROUP BY, COUNT/SUM/AVG/MAX/MIN, HAVING, window functions intro
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Raw SELECT returns individual rows. But business questions are often about groups: 'how many orders per customer?', 'what is the average order value per month?', 'which product category has the highest revenue?'. Aggregations summarize sets of rows into single values.
whyItExists.solution: GROUP BY splits rows into groups. Aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN) compute a value for each group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation. Window functions compute aggregates without collapsing rows.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Any time you need a summary: totals, counts, averages, rankings. Dashboard metrics, reporting, analytics queries.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't aggregate in the database what you can calculate from a single row. And don't aggregate in the database what you can precalculate into a summary table for frequently-run expensive aggregations.

explainModes.beginner: GROUP BY is like sorting your rows into buckets, then calculating something about each bucket. 'How many orders per customer?' — put all orders in buckets by customer, then COUNT each bucket. 'What is the total revenue per month?' — bucket orders by month, then SUM the revenue in each bucket.
explainModes.standard: Aggregate functions operate on a set of rows and return a single value per group. NULL values are ignored by aggregate functions (except COUNT(*)). COUNT(*) counts rows including NULLs; COUNT(column) counts non-NULL values. HAVING is like WHERE but for groups — it filters after GROUP BY. Window functions (OVER) compute aggregates across a sliding window without collapsing rows — perfect for running totals, rankings, and comparing each row to its neighbors.
explainModes.technical: The query planner implements GROUP BY with either a HashAggregate (builds a hash table of group keys) or a GroupAggregate (uses sorted input). HashAggregate is faster for low-cardinality groups; GroupAggregate is used when the input is already sorted. Window functions run after GROUP BY but before ORDER BY — they see the full result of aggregations. FILTER (WHERE ...) on aggregate functions allows conditional aggregation without a CASE expression.

content.code:
-- Count all rows
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;

-- Count non-null values in a column
SELECT COUNT(coupon_code) FROM orders;  -- only counts rows with a coupon

-- Sum, average, min, max
SELECT
  SUM(total_price)    AS revenue,
  AVG(total_price)    AS avg_order,
  MIN(total_price)    AS smallest_order,
  MAX(total_price)    AS largest_order
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed';

-- Orders per customer
SELECT
  user_id,
  COUNT(*) AS order_count,
  SUM(total_price) AS total_spent
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

-- Revenue by month
SELECT
  DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at) AS month,
  COUNT(*) AS orders,
  SUM(total_price) AS revenue
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY DATE_TRUNC('month', created_at)
ORDER BY month;

-- Group by multiple columns
SELECT
  category,
  status,
  COUNT(*) AS count
FROM products
GROUP BY category, status
ORDER BY category, count DESC;

-- WHERE filters rows before grouping
-- HAVING filters groups after grouping

-- Find customers who spent more than $500 total
SELECT
  user_id,
  SUM(total_price) AS total_spent
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed'          -- filter rows first
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING SUM(total_price) > 500.00    -- then filter groups
ORDER BY total_spent DESC;

content.text: Window functions — aggregates without collapsing rows

content.code:
-- Running total of revenue
SELECT
  id,
  created_at,
  total_price,
  SUM(total_price) OVER (ORDER BY created_at) AS running_total
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'completed';

-- Rank customers by total spending
SELECT
  user_id,
  SUM(total_price) AS total_spent,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(total_price) DESC) AS spending_rank
FROM orders
GROUP BY user_id;

-- Each order as a % of the customer's total
SELECT
  id,
  user_id,
  total_price,
  ROUND(
    100.0 * total_price / SUM(total_price) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id), 2
  ) AS pct_of_customer_total
FROM orders;

questions.question: You want to find all categories that have more than 10 products. Which clause filters by this condition?
questions.explanation: HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. You cannot use aggregate functions in WHERE because WHERE is evaluated before grouping. The correct query: SELECT category, COUNT(*) FROM products GROUP BY category HAVING COUNT(*) > 10.

faq.q: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
faq.a: COUNT(*) counts every row including those with NULL values. COUNT(column) counts only the rows where that column is NOT NULL. Example: if 5 of 100 orders have no coupon, COUNT(*) returns 100 but COUNT(coupon_code) returns 95.

examples: DATE_TRUNC('month', timestamp) is used to group time-series data by month or week in analytics dashboards
Window functions power leaderboards, ranking pages, and 'top N per category' queries that would otherwise require complex subqueries
